title: A Choir for the Winter
premise: Folklorist Orsen Halloran arrives in the snowbound village of Vellamoor to record its winter songs, only to find the villagers refuse to sing any verse twice — and every photograph in her grandmother's old house now shows an extra chair at the table, with her grandmother seated in it. As the frost spreads inward from the windows in deliberate patterns, Orsen discovers the village founders bound a hungry presence beneath the church with a sung ritual, renewed each generation by twelve voices. The last choir died in 1963, and the binding is failing; the extra chair is the presence's invitation, and her grandmother's return is its lure. To survive, Orsen must gather eleven reluctant villagers, teach them the forbidden verses, and complete the ritual before the final frost pattern closes — but the price of survival is that one voice must remain behind, singing forever, and Orsen chooses to let the chair take her instead of the child who was meant to fill it.
about_author: Petra Kavanagh is a former church organist from northern England who spent a decade collecting disappearing folk songs before turning to horror. She writes in unheated rooms, on the theory that cold keeps the sentences honest.

chapters.title: The Verse They Won't Repeat
chapters.summary: Orsen Halloran's POV. Arriving in Vellamoor during the first snowfall, Orsen records an elderly singer who stops mid-verse, pale, refusing to sing it again. The villagers are polite but watchful. Emotional beat: curiosity curdling into unease as she realizes the whole village shares one unspoken fear.

chapters.title: Grandmother's House, Grandmother's Rules
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. She inherits and moves into her late grandmother's cottage, finding wax-sealed doors, salt lines, and a notebook of songs annotated 'never twice.' That night, all the family photographs show an extra chair at the table. Emotional beat: grief complicated by dread — the house knew something she didn't.

chapters.title: Twelve Chairs, Eleven Voices
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV, interleaved with her grandmother's journal entries. Research reveals the Founders' Choir: twelve singers who bound something beneath the church in 1781, renewed every generation until the choir died in 1963. The photographs now show twelve chairs. Emotional beat: the thrill of discovery giving way to horror at what the songs were for.

chapters.title: What the Frost Is Writing
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Frost patterns on her windows form musical notation — verses from the forbidden song, slightly wrong, inviting correction. Her grandmother appears in a new photograph, seated in the twelfth chair, looking directly out. Emotional beat: isolation deepening as the supernatural turns personal and intimate.

chapters.title: The Ones Who Remember Singing
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: Orsen and Ivo Tarn, the gravedigger whose father died in the 1963 choir. He confirms the binding is failing — livestock gone silent, children sleepwalking toward the church. Emotional beat: the first fragile alliance; found family beginning to form around shared terror.

chapters.title: A Rehearsal of the Damned
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. She persuades eleven villagers to rehearse in secret, but the first full run-through makes the church bells toll untouched and the frost race across every window in town. One singer flees; the presence speaks through the hymn board. Emotional beat: hope undercut by proof that singing summons as much as it binds.

chapters.title: The Chair in the Middle
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. The extra chair physically manifests in Orsen's kitchen, warm as a lap. Her grandmother's voice uses the radio to beg her to sit. Orsen nearly does; Ivo drags her back. Emotional beat: the corruption of love — the presence weaponizes longing for family against them both.

chapters.title: One Voice Short
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. The fleeing singer is found frozen mid-note outside the church; the frost has written its penultimate pattern. The ritual needs twelve living voices tonight or the binding breaks at dawn. A child, Maren, volunteers — she hears the song 'singing itself' in her head. Emotional beat: desperation and guilt; survival demands a sacrifice no one will name.

chapters.title: The Final Pattern
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs converging. In the freezing church, the eleven sing the forbidden verses as the presence rises through the floor, wearing the faces of the dead choir. Maren begins the twelfth line. Orsen sees the truth: the ritual doesn't banish the presence — it feeds it one keeper. Emotional beat: climax — terror transfigured into terrible clarity.

chapters.title: A Choir for the Winter
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV, then epilogue letters. She takes Maren's place mid-verse, sitting down in the twelfth chair as the frost completes its pattern and stills. Spring comes to Vellamoor; Ivo raises Maren, and the village sings once more — never twice. In the church photographs, twelve chairs, one occupied. Emotional beat: bittersweet resolution — found family forged, power paid for, survival purchased at the highest price.
